Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis
Details:
- Failing test: EntitiesTest.testNumberOverflow() expects that unescaping a numeric entity whose value exceeds the maximum Java char (0xFFFF) leaves the input unchanged:
  - doTestUnescapeEntity("&#12345678;", "&#12345678;")
  - The helper asserts both Entities.unescape(String) and Entities.unescape(Writer, String) behave this way.

- Issue summary: unescapeXml("&#12345678;") should produce "&#12345678;". Rationale: maximum value for a Java char is 0xFFFF; higher numeric entity references are invalid in this context and should not be converted.

- Code analysis:
  - org.apache.commons.lang.Entities.unescape(String):
    - Parses numeric entities (decimal or hex) into an int (lines ~843–852).
    - Only sets entityValue = -1 on parse failure or empty content.
    - If entityValue != -1, it appends (char) (entityValue) (lines 861–863).
    - There is no range check to detect values > 0xFFFF. For an input like "&#12345678;", parseInt succeeds (value fits in int), so entityValue is 12345678; it then casts to char, truncating to the low 16 bits and producing an unintended character instead of leaving the entity unchanged.

  - org.apache.commons.lang.Entities.unescape(Writer, String):
    - Similar logic: parses numeric entities into an int (lines 912–924).
    - If entityValue != -1, it calls writer.write(entityValue) (line 938), which writes a single 16‑bit char (low 16 bits of the int).
    - Again, there is no range check; oversized values are incorrectly written as truncated chars instead of being treated as invalid and left verbatim.

- How the bug manifests:
  - For "&#12345678;" and similar inputs, parsing yields a valid int > 0xFFFF. Because the code lacks a bounds check, it treats the entity as valid and converts it to a char via truncation, changing the input.
  - The test expects such entities to be considered invalid and preserved as-is. Hence, the assertions fail for both the String-returning and Writer-based unescape paths.

- Root cause:
  - Missing validation that a parsed numeric entity falls within the valid Java char range (0x0000–0xFFFF). Oversized values should be marked invalid (entityValue = -1) so the original entity text is preserved.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
